questions.q: In the 1880s, why did physicists insist that the luminiferous aether had to exist?
options: It was needed to explain why light travels faster than sound
Every other wave they knew was a disturbance moving through a material, so light — being a wave — was assumed to need a medium too
Maxwell's equations contained a term that could only mean a solid substance filled space
It was the only way to explain why the Earth orbits the Sun
questions.explanation: The argument was by analogy: sound waves move through air, water waves through water, so a light wave seemed to need something to wave in. The aether was imagined as a transparent, weightless, perfectly elastic substance filling all of space — and crucially, the one thing truly at absolute rest. The tempting wrong answer about Maxwell's equations is backwards: Maxwell's equations gave the speed of light but did not require a material medium.

questions.q: Why should there be an 'aether wind' that the experiment could detect?
options: Because the Sun radiates aether outward in all directions

Because the Earth races through the supposedly stationary aether at about 30 km/s, so an observer on Earth should feel a stream of aether flowing past — like the wind a motorcyclist feels on a still day
Because the aether is heated by sunlight and rises like a convection current
Because light pushes the aether ahead of it as it travels
questions.explanation: If the aether sits still and the Earth ploughs through it at its orbital speed of ~30 km/s, then relative to Earth there should be a steady aether wind blowing past, exactly as a rider on a calm day feels an apparent wind from their own motion. Detecting it would let you measure the Earth's absolute motion through space.

questions.q: In the Michelson interferometer, what physically produces the pattern of bright and dark interference fringes?
options: The beam splitter changes the colour of one of the two beams
The two recombining beams add as waves: where crests line up they reinforce (bright), and where they fall out of step they cancel (dark)
One mirror absorbs more light than the other, creating shadows
The mercury bath bends the light as the stone rotates
questions.explanation: A beam splitter divides one beam into two perpendicular arms; each reflects off a mirror and returns to recombine. Because light is a wave, the recombined beams add — crest-on-crest gives a bright band, out-of-step gives a dark band. Shifting one beam's timing by even half a wavelength (~250 billionths of a metre) slides a bright fringe to where a dark one was, making the device extraordinarily sensitive.

questions.q: The 1887 experiment gave a null result. What did this null result actually establish?
options: That the aether definitely does not exist anywhere in the universe
That the Earth is not moving through the aether at its orbital speed — light travelled at the same speed in every direction regardless of how the apparatus was pointed
That the interferometer was too crude to detect any motion
That light is a particle rather than a wave
questions.explanation: The result was narrower and stranger than 'no aether'. It proved the Earth is not moving through a stationary aether at orbital speed: no aether wind appeared, so light kept the same speed in every arm and direction. The instrument could catch one-fortieth of the expected effect and caught essentially nothing.

questions.q: How did FitzGerald (and later Lorentz) try to rescue the aether theory from the null result?
options: By proposing that the Earth drags a thick blanket of aether with it everywhere it goes
By proposing that any object moving through the aether physically contracts along its direction of motion, shortening the parallel arm by exactly enough to cancel the expected time difference
By proving Michelson's mirrors were misaligned
By arguing that light slows down inside the beam splitter glass
questions.explanation: FitzGerald's one-paragraph idea (1889) was that motion through the aether squeezes matter along the line of travel. The arm pointing into the wind shrinks by just the right amount to cancel the slower light, so the round trips come out equal and the fringes do not shift. The contraction is undetectable because your measuring rulers shrink along with everything else.

questions.q: According to the episode, did Einstein build special relativity directly on the Michelson-Morley experiment?
options: Yes — his 1905 paper cites it as the central piece of evidence
No — his 1905 paper does not even cite it; he reached relativity mainly through theory, and the tidy 'experiment inspired the theory' story was largely stitched together afterwards
Yes — he repeated the experiment himself before writing the paper
No — he never heard of the experiment and rejected its conclusion
questions.explanation: This is one of the great myths of physics. Einstein's 1905 'On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies' does not cite Michelson-Morley; he arrived at relativity through discomfort with how Maxwell's electromagnetism and Newton's mechanics fit together, citing other evidence like light in flowing water and stellar aberration. The experiment did not cause the theory — but it stands as the most powerful evidence that the theory is right.

questions.q: From memory: state Einstein's two postulates of special relativity, and explain how each one accounts for the Michelson-Morley null result.
keyPoints: Principle of relativity: all inertial frames of reference are equivalent — the laws of physics are identical for any observer moving at constant velocity.
Constancy of light speed: the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for every observer, independent of the motion of the source or observer.
Constancy of c means light has the same speed in both arms, so there is no time difference and no fringe shift.
Equivalence of inertial frames means there is no aether rest frame, so it cannot matter which way the apparatus points — rotating it produces no change in the pattern.
questions.explanation: NESA does not fix which postulate is numbered first, so state BOTH precisely. If you also linked constancy of c to 'same speed in both arms' and equivalence of frames to 'direction cannot matter', grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: From memory: why is the Michelson-Morley experiment described as 'the most important failure in the history of physics', and what is its modern legacy?
keyPoints: It set out to detect the aether and measure the Earth's motion through it, but found a clean, precise null result — nothing.
A sufficiently precise 'nothing' was worth more than a thousand confirmations: it pointed to there being no aether, no absolute rest, no fixed stage in the cosmos.
The Lorentz transformations it provoked, reinterpreted by Einstein, became the bedrock of modern physics (including E = mc²).
Michelson's interferometer design lives on in LIGO, which detected gravitational waves in 2015.
questions.explanation: Reward yourself for capturing both the irony (a 'failure' that found nothing) and the payoff (no aether/absolute rest, plus the interferometer's legacy in LIGO). The instrument built to find the aether and failed went on, a century later, to hear the universe ringing.

questions.q: Using the 1887 figures from the episode — effective arm length L = 11 m, Earth's speed v = 3.0 x 10^4 m/s, speed of light c = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s, and light wavelength lambda = 5.0 x 10^-7 m — estimate the expected fringe shift n on a 90 degree rotation, using n = 2Lv^2 / (lambda c^2).
questions.explanation: This is the ~0.4 fringe shift quoted in the 1887 paper. Squaring the speeds gives 9.0 x 10^8 on top and 9.0 x 10^16 below; the result is just under half a fringe — and the instrument could detect a shift as small as 0.01 fringe, so the signal should have been unmissable.

questions.q: The episode says the expected shift was about 0.40 of a fringe and that Michelson and Morley could detect a shift as small as about 0.01 of a fringe. How many times larger than their detection limit was the signal they were hunting for?
questions.given: expected shift \(\approx 0.40\) fringe,  smallest detectable shift \(\approx 0.01\) fringe
questions.explanation: The signal they expected was about 40 times larger than the smallest shift their instrument could resolve, which is why they were so confident they could not miss it. Pointed at the aether wind, the instrument nonetheless read essentially zero — the paper stated the displacement was certainly less than a twentieth, probably less than a fortieth, of the expected amount.
